---
title: "Research"
---

My research is in experimental linguistics: phonetics, laboratory phonology, and psycholinguistics. I study how listeners use prosodic and voice-quality cues, such as tone, intonation, and phonation, in real-time spoken language processing, and how those cues are represented. I use laboratory and field experiments, acoustic analysis, and statistical modeling. I also apply these methods to language-related data science projects.

## Current projects

### Thai phonation and voice quality

Building on my previous work, this research examines phonation as an additional cue in Thai tone and intonation. It began as a descriptive look at how voice quality varies across tones and intonational contexts, and I’m now exploring how that variation can be modeled and how listeners use it in processing.

### LanguageFinder

LanguageFinder was started by [Catherine Brockway](https://geoling.github.io), and I’ve continued developing it with [Connor Flynn](https://connorflynn.github.io) and students. It’s an interactive Shiny app that maps language use and English proficiency across communities using custom-tabulated American Community Survey data from the U.S. Census Bureau, at the state, county, and tract levels. A team of Chaminade data science students extended it as their capstone, presenting at the Nā Liko Naʻauao symposium in 2026.

## Past projects

### Thai tone & intonation

How do lexical tone and sentence intonation interact in Thai, and which acoustic cues do listeners use to process each? I addressed this through a categorical perception study, a production study, and an eye-tracking study of real-time processing. Supervised by Amy Schafer (University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa)

### Stress in Pidgin (Hawaiʻi Creole)

Acoustic correlates of word-level stress in Pidgin, as a first step toward describing Pidgin intonation.

### Structural probabilities in speech production in Japanese

With [Nozomi Tanaka](https://nozomitanaka.com/), a study of whether structural predictability in Japanese relative clauses shapes word duration during incremental production. Presented at ICPhS 2019. [Read the proceedings](https://ambercamp.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/icphs0967.pdf "icphs0967").

### Nasality in Lakota

With [Ryan E. Henke](https://ryanhenke.com), a study of whether orthography helps naive learners perceive the Lakota nasal vowel contrast, with implications for language revitalization teaching. [Presented at ICLDC 2019](https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/handle/10125/44813).
